Armor and clothing occupy the same five body locations @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.JJ04T5LHImjlILs1]{Chapter 7} uses for called shots — Head, Torso, Legs, Hands, and Feet. Each location is covered by one Armor Piece: a fixed combination of a Plate (a Volume and Base DR set by Location and Tier) and a Material (a Density, Cost, and DR Multiplier chosen from Step 1). Weight, cost, and DR for every Location/Tier/Material combination are worked out in the Step 2 catalog, so a Piece is simply selected off the table and worn — no arithmetic is done at the table. A Suit is any combination of Armor Pieces worn together; the preconstructed sets later in this chapter (Combat Suit, Beskar'gam, Republic Trooper, etc.) are simply popular combinations built the same way.

Hands and Feet are priced per extremity. A Hand Plate or Glove covers one hand; a Foot Plate or Boot covers one foot. The Step 2 catalog price and weight are for a single item, so a two-handed, two-footed character buys two of each — and because that is the ordinary case, a character sheet or shop should offer the full set by default, one per limb, quantity taken from the character's own anatomy rather than assumed to be two.

Single Purchases: Buying or crafting a single one is always allowed: a character with one hand buys one Glove, a four-armed character buys four, and nothing stops a player fitting a Glove on one hand and a Gauntlet weapon (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.gxAN3kXd5U4q1H3c]{Chapter 11}) on the other, or different materials left and right.

Location Pieces: Head, Torso and Legs are location Pieces rather than per-extremity ones: one Head Plate covers the head, one Leg Plate covers both legs, exactly as @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.JJ04T5LHImjlILs1]{Chapter 7}'s hit locations treat them.

Color and finish are free. Any Armor Piece, Clothing Piece, cloak or accessory can be made in any color, pattern or finish the player likes at no change to weight, cost, DR or any other statistic — dye, paint, etching, clan markings, unit insignia, weathering, a mirror polish. Bought items come however the player wants them; crafted or recolored items need a Dedicated Workshop or better (see Coloring under Shared Skills & Workspace). Where this chapter names a color (Jedi robes in tan and brown, Mandalorian plate in clan colors, Republic Trooper white), that is the conventional look, not a requirement: it tells you what people expect to see, and wearing something else may draw attention, but it never changes the numbers. Only a material change alters an item's statistics.

Default appearance. An item with no color specified looks like the material it is made of. Rigid materials: Durasteel is dull gunmetal gray; Plasteel is off-white with a faint sheen; Duraplast is matte pale gray; Flex-Armor is dark charcoal, slightly rubbery; Ballistic Threading is drab olive or gray weave; Scrap Metal is mismatched, rusted and pitted; Phrik is dark silver-blue; Beskar is bright polished silver. Soft goods: Synth-Cloth is undyed beige; Synth-Leather is mid-brown; Synthmesh is dark gray; Plastoid is bone white; Armorweave is deep charcoal with a faint iridescence; Synth-Silk is pearl. A Piece built from more than one material shows the Shell's color unless the player says otherwise.

1. Raw Materials — bought or salvaged by the pound (Durasteel, Beskar, etc. — see Step 1). Used only when crafting a new Armor Piece.

2. Armor Pieces — the finished, wearable items. Each is a fixed combination of Location, Tier, and Material with its DR, Weight, and Cost worked out in the Step 2 catalog. These are what a character actually carries in inventory.

3. Suits — any combination of Armor Pieces, one per body location, worn together. Total weight and cost are added directly; each location keeps its own independent DR. See Assembling a Suit below.

Named armor sets (Combat Suit, Republic Trooper, Mandalorian Beskar'gam, etc.) are popular combinations of Armor Pieces, not fixed bundles a character must take or leave as a whole. A character may wear a Beskar'gam Torso, a Republic Trooper Standard Helmet, custom Scrap Metal boots, and gloves from an entirely different tier in the same outfit. Any Piece — catalog or custom-built — may be worn in its slot regardless of what's worn in every other slot.

Example: Head — Republic Trooper Standard Helmet (DR 7, Plasteel). Torso — Heavy Torso Plate (Beskar) (DR 30). Legs — a custom Light Leg Plate (Scrap Metal), scavenged (DR 2). Hands — Medium Hand Plate (Plasteel), purchased (DR 4, built from the Custom Piece formula). Feet — Combat Suit Boots (DR 4, Durasteel). Weight and Cost are simply added across the chosen Pieces, as in the Assembling a Suit example below.

Clothing vs. Armor: Slot & Layering Rules

Armor Weight Class: A piece’s weight class -- Light, Medium, or Heavy -- is set by which catalog tier (see the tables below) it’s built or bought from, not by a strict weight cutoff. As a rule of thumb: Light pieces usually run under 5 lbs for DR 3-5; Medium usually runs 5-9 lbs for DR 5-18; Heavy usually runs 15-25 lbs for DR 15-30. A few premium materials break this pattern -- Duraplast, for instance, hits Heavy-tier DR at a fraction of the usual weight -- but these still count as their catalog tier (not their raw weight) for Armor skill (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.aHFgSZUXNODEwQd2]{Chapter 3}) and Encumbrance (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.JJ04T5LHImjlILs1]{Chapter 7}) purposes.

Armor as a Sum of Its Parts: Every Armor Piece is built from up to five components — Shell (the plate itself, cut from the material catalog below), Backing (the padding/strapping layer that secures the Shell), Frame/Mounting (structural hardware determining Mod Slot count), Visor (Head only, and only when Sealed), and Trim (an optional lining). Every one of these has its own weight and cost, and every Piece in the Step 2 catalog shows its full construction — component by component, from raw material forward. These are pre-built, catalog-listed parts: a crafter builds "Torso Backing" as a whole item from the recipe in Building New Armor Pieces, not by hand-mixing raw Synthmesh and Silicon in arbitrary ratios. What a player customizes is which finished parts they combine into a full Piece.

One base layer per location. Each hit location (see the Hit Locations table below) holds exactly one base-layer item: either a Clothing item (DR 0) or an Armor Piece (Light/Medium/Heavy). An Armor Piece is assumed to already include its own lining/fit — you don't stack a Clothing item and an Armor Piece in the same location at the same time.

Utility & Accessories are a separate layer. Belts, cloaks, holsters, bandoliers, jetpacks, and similar Utility/Accessory items are worn over or alongside the base layer and are never blocked by it — a character can wear a Belt and a Cloak regardless of whether their Torso slot holds a Basic Tunic or a Heavy Torso Plate (Beskar). The Body Glove Utility item is the sole exception built to go underneath a Sealed Head/Torso Piece, as noted on those Pieces.

Mods live inside a specific Piece. Underlayer/Overlay/Integrated/Utility Components (Blunt Force Padding, Cortosis Weave, etc.) are installed into one specific Armor Piece at crafting time, up to that Piece's Mod Slot limit. They aren't separately worn items — but per the existing rule, they can be added or swapped after the fact with a successful technology skill roll (or a vendor/technician) rather than being fixed forever.

Damage, Degradation & Condition States

Because every body location is now its own independent Piece, condition is tracked per Piece, not per suit — grinding your Torso Plate down to Broken doesn't touch your Leg Plate's condition. Otherwise this is the same four-state system used for weapons and shields (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.JJ04T5LHImjlILs1]{Chapter 7}: Combat).

Damage, Degradation & Condition States
StateEffect
FineFunctions exactly as listed — full DR/Dur.
DamagedDR reduced by a flat 25% (round down) when reached via a Major Wound; ordinary hits track DR loss directly instead (see Taking Damage, above). Environmental seals still function.
BrokenDR 0. Environmental seals fail (Sealed traits stop working).
DestroyedPermanently ruined. Stripped of all Mod Slots. Can only be broken down via the Salvaging rules below.

Taking Damage: whenever a hit to a given location deals HP damage that exceeds that location’s current Piece DR, the Piece’s DR permanently drops by 1 (cumulative). This tracked loss is the entire effect of an ordinary hit — it does not additionally trigger the Condition Table’s percentage effect. Clothing uses its Dur (default 10) in place of DR on the exact same track.

Condition Shifts: a Piece’s condition is a label read directly off its current DR: at or above its listed value, it’s Fine; below listed value (from the tracking above), Damaged; at 0, Broken. Any further hit to a Broken Piece destroys it. This labeling doesn’t add a further DR penalty on top of the tracking above. All of this tracking runs on the Piece’s own DR, never on a Mod’s conditional bonus. A Mod adds its bonus to whatever DR the Piece currently has against the damage type it names; the bonus itself does not degrade, and it is not part of the number the condition label is read off -- a Torso Plate at DR 0 is Broken even wearing Cortosis Weave, and its Mods stop contributing with it.

Major Wounds: a Major Wound (a single blow dealing ≥ half the wearer’s total HP) on a protected location drops that location’s Piece down one full condition step immediately, regardless of the DR math above — applying the Condition Table’s effect directly (Damaged: DR reduced by a flat 25%, round down) if that’s worse than the Piece’s current tracked DR. Ordinary hits and Major Wounds never both apply to the same point of damage.

Field Repairs: Armoury (Body Armor) or Mechanic, 10 minutes per Piece. Margin of success 3+ restores a Damaged Piece to Fine. Broken or Destroyed Pieces can't be field-repaired — see Deconstructing/Salvaging under Fabrication, Modification & Salvage.

Size Modifier (SM) Multiplier

This single multiplier table is used everywhere in this chapter that scales for a non-standard Size Modifier -- Armor Pieces, Clothing, and Belts alike -- so it typically only needs to be looked up once per character. The one exception is an individual limb with its own, different effective SM (see Armor for Non-Standard Physiologies later in this chapter), which uses this same table a second time.

Size Modifier (SM) Multiplier
SM-2-10+0.35+0.75+1+2+3
1.0xMultiplier0.5x0.7x1.14x1.33x1.5x2.0x3.0x

Which governs: the table above is the multiplier, and every figure this book scales by SM is derived from it. The formula behind it is Multiplier = 10^(SM ÷ 6) -- ten raised to the power of (SM divided by 6), not multiplied -- and it reproduces the fractional species rows exactly (+0.35 gives 1.1438, +0.75 gives 1.3335), while the whole-number rows are rounded to the friendlier figures printed above. Use the table for any SM it lists; use the formula -- never interpolation between the printed rows -- to derive a Size Modifier the table does not list, and round it to two decimals.

Materials are only referenced when a crafter builds a new Armor Piece for the catalog below — a one-time calculation, not something players manage during play.

Tailoring & Fitting

Scaling a brand-new Piece: Final Weight = Catalog Weight × SM Multiplier. Final Cost = Catalog Cost × SM Multiplier. DR does not change — a bigger suit of the same tier and material protects exactly as well, it just takes proportionally more material to cover the extra area.

What Goes on the Sheet: The scaled figure, not the catalog one. A catalog price is what the item costs at SM 0; what a character records is what they paid, which for a non-standard size is the scaled weight and the cost derived from it.

Example: Rokarr's Fatigue Boots are a 26 CR catalog line and a 34 CR entry on his sheet, and his equipment total counts the 34. The catalog figure never appears on a character sheet except for an SM 0 character, where the two are the same number.

Rounding: Scale the weight first and round it to two decimal places -- that rounded weight is what goes on the sheet and what the cost derives from, so a 0.5 lb shirt at ×1.33 becomes 0.67 lb, not 0.665, and prices at 0.67 × 10 × 1.5 = 11 CR rather than 10. Carrying the unrounded weight through to the price gives a different answer on about a third of scaled garments.

Fitting an existing (looted, purchased, or hand-me-down) Piece is a different situation, with its own penalties and alteration costs: Minor and Major Alterations below cover Size Modifier changes. For adapting a Piece to a different limb count or placement, see Armor for Non-Standard Physiologies (Anatomical Overhaul) later in this chapter.

Fitting Penalty: Armor or Clothing built more than 1 full SM point away from the wearer’s own SM (e.g., wearer SM 0, Piece built for SM +1) cannot be worn without the Mis-Sized penalty (-2 DX / -1 Basic Move); 2 or more full SM points away, it can’t be worn at all. This is measured in whole SM points, not rows on the SM Multiplier table -- a Piece built for SM +0.35 or +0.75 counts as less than 1 point away from SM 0, not as separate steps.

Tailoring & Fitting
Fit ProblemPenalty / Fix
Wrong build, same SM"Ill-Fitting": -1 DX and -1 Basic Move until altered.
Wrong SM (1 step off)"Mis-Sized": -2 DX and -1 Basic Move until altered.
Wrong SM (2+ steps off)Cannot be worn at all.

Minor Alterations (same SM, different build — adjusting straps and internal padding): Armoury (Body Armor)/Armstech (armor’s weight class) for rigid Pieces or Sewing for flexible ones. Negligible materials, 2 hours, unmodified skill roll. Success removes the Ill-Fitting penalty. Failure leaves it Ill-Fitting. Critical Failure reduces the Piece's DR by 20% (round down) until repaired.

Major Alterations (changing SM entirely): requires a dedicated workshop. Costs 20–50% of the Piece's final base cost in labor; ×1.5 time if the Piece's DR is 15+. Scaling down needs no new material. Scaling up requires paying for the added material weight difference at the Piece's material Cost/lb.

Clothing is cheaper to alter: Sewing skill, and tailoring labor costs only 10–20% of the item's final base cost, regardless of direction.

Market price = Material Value × 2; Finished Item Price = (component sum + 20 CR per CP of any traits the gadget grants) × 2 for Phase 2, then × 3 for the Datacard Flashing phase -- the same chain as Belts, ×6 over the component sum. A catalogued Function Firmware Datacard below is priced as medium plus content: the blank card's 174 CR (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.Skjt6Gqhhw8BiF1Y]{Chapter 10}) plus that program's Programming Fee, and it weighs the card's 0.28 lb, firmware having no weight of its own. A finished gadget pays the fee only -- the card is the crafter's tool and does not stay in the item.

Every Piece in the catalog above assumes a standard bipedal build -- two arms, two legs, two hands, two feet, one head. This section covers any departure from that baseline: fewer limbs, more limbs, differently-sized limbs, or non-standard placement.

Per-Limb Coverage (Legs, Hands, Feet, Head)

Hand Plate, Foot Plate, Gloves and Boots are already priced per extremity (see the note at the start of this chapter), so a character simply buys one per hand or foot — two for the usual anatomy, one for a character with one hand, four for a four-armed species, none at all where the limb is absent. No halving or doubling is involved; the listed figure is what one costs. Leg Plate covers both legs as a single location Piece, and Head Plate is priced per head — a multi-headed character buys one Head Plate per head. A species with legs in a non-standard arrangement (a centaur's four, a serpentine tail) buys Leg Plates at the listed rate per pair, or the GM prices a bespoke Piece from Building New Armor Pieces.

Losing a Covered Limb in Combat

If a limb is severed per @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.JJ04T5LHImjlILs1]{Chapter 7}’s Severing Threshold rules, the armor or clothing covering that specific limb is severed with it in the same blow -- this is not a later alteration or a trip to a workshop, it happens automatically as part of the wound. For a Leg Plate (already treated as two independent per-limb halves, above), losing one leg means losing that half’s DR and coverage; the remaining leg’s protection is untouched. For a Torso Plate’s sleeve, losing an arm removes that arm’s DR coverage only -- the Torso DR itself, and any other sleeve, are unaffected.

Value afterward differs by piece type. A Leg Plate missing one leg’s half is now worth exactly its per-limb baseline value (the original listed price ÷ 2, per Per-Limb Coverage above) -- it is physically and functionally half of what it was. A Torso Plate missing a sleeve keeps its full listed value: the Arm DR formula never priced the sleeve as its own component, so the Torso material itself (DR, weight, cost) is unchanged -- it simply no longer protects a second arm. The severed portion itself can be salvaged, not Deconstructed (combat damage leaves it too irregular for a clean teardown) -- use the same process as Salvaging Armor Pieces, applied to its per-limb baseline value: 50% raw material recovered on a Success, 75% on a Critical Success, 0% on a Failure.

Arms

Standard two-arm coverage is free, riding on the Torso Plate's built-in Arm DR formula (Arm DR = ⌊Torso DR × 0.65⌋). Extra or unusual arms work like this:

One arm costs no less. The Torso Plate doesn't shrink; the unused sleeve simply goes unused.

A third or further arm needs an Auxiliary Sleeve. Price it at a quarter of the listed, matched-pair Leg Plate weight and cost -- half of one leg's per-unit share, since an arm is roughly half a leg's surface area -- built from the same material and tier as the rest of the suit, and providing the same Arm DR formula as the Torso's built-in sleeves.

A sleeveless Torso Plate extends nothing. With no Arm DR of its own it has no Auxiliary Sleeve to extend, and buys none for any extra arm.

No comparable catalog entry, no charge. If the Torso is homebrew or GM-built and no catalog Leg Plate matches its material and tier, the Auxiliary Sleeve costs nothing rather than an invented figure. Price it properly once a comparable entry exists.

Extra arms of differing size. The two least expensive to cover -- typically the standard-sized ones -- ride free on the Torso's built-in coverage. Only the remaining, oddly-sized arms are billed for an Auxiliary Sleeve, plus any size adjustment from Oversized or Undersized Limbs, below.

Oversized or Undersized Limbs

If one specific limb is notably larger or smaller than a standard limb of its type -- independent of the character’s overall SM -- assign that limb its own effective SM relative to a normal limb, and apply the SM Multiplier table (Step 1) to its per-limb baseline weight and cost from above.

Placement

A center or rear-center limb costs the same as any other extra limb of its type (above). Placement is a targeting question (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.JJ04T5LHImjlILs1]{Chapter 7}: Extra Limbs, Cybernetics, and Non-Human Hit Locations), not an Armor pricing one.

Gauntlets and Boots

Both items physically extend past the single Hit Location they’re named for -- a Gauntlet up the forearm, a Boot up the calf -- but this chapter keeps limb loss simple rather than tracking exactly where along a limb a cut landed. The rule is the same as any other slot: if the Hand Hit Location is severed, the Gauntlet is lost with it, full stop, the same as a Hand Plate or a glove. It does not matter that the housing was strapped to the forearm -- that distinction is a fitting/mounting detail, not a reason to keep the item equipped once its slot is gone.

A Boot follows the identical rule, in reverse: if the Foot Hit Location is severed, the Boot goes with it, the same as Foot Plate itself (see Losing a Covered Limb in Combat, above). No separate ruling is needed for whether the cut landed above or below the boot’s shaft -- losing the Foot location loses everything built for that slot, cleanly, without introducing new Hit Locations this chapter doesn’t otherwise track.

Tailoring Existing Armor to a New Physiology

Adapting a looted, purchased, or hand-me-down Piece to a limb count or placement it wasn’t built for is its own alteration type, alongside the Minor and Major (SM) Alterations above: Anatomical Overhaul. Requires a dedicated workshop and an Armoury (Body Armor)/Armstech (armor’s weight class)/Sewing roll, following the same time and labor-cost structure as a Major Alteration. Material cost equals the relevant per-limb baseline weight (from above) for each limb being added or adapted, at the Piece’s material Cost/lb. Until this is done, Armor that isn’t tailored to the wearer’s actual limb configuration cannot be worn at all -- the same hard block as being two or more Size Modifiers away.

text.content:
Every Armor Piece in this chapter is built from up to five components, and every one of them has its own weight and cost. Nothing is abstracted away: the tables in Step 2 are the finished results of the derivation below, and any Piece can be traced back to the raw material it was cut from. This is a one-time job for whoever expands the catalog, not something players do per-suit — but the work is shown so it can be checked, extended, or rebuilt at any time.

Component 1 — Shell (the plate itself, every location). Weight = Plate Volume × the material's Density. Value = Shell Weight × the material's Cost/lb. Plate Volume is fixed by Location and Tier (see the reference table below); the material is the crafter's choice, restricted by tier availability (Step 1). A material whose Step 1 entry names no tier is available at all three; where it names one or two, those are the only tiers it can be worked at, and no Piece exists outside them.

Component 2 — Backing (the padding and strapping layer that secures the Shell, every location). A fixed, pre-built part: its weight and value depend only on Location, never on tier or material.

  • Head 0.42 lbs (11 CR)
  • Torso 1.00 lbs (27 CR)
  • Leg 1.00 lbs (27 CR)
  • Hand 0.19 lbs (4.5 CR)
  • Foot 0.31 lbs (8 CR).

A Backing may instead be built Wired, carrying 0.15 lbs of Silicon (50 CR/lb, as the Circuits below) run through the layer as conductor:

  • Wired Head 0.57 lbs (18.5 CR)
  • Wired Torso 1.15 lbs (34.5 CR)
  • Wired Leg 1.15 lbs (34.5 CR)
  • Wired Hand 0.34 lbs (12 CR)
  • Wired Foot 0.46 lbs (15.5 CR).

A Wired Backing lets its Piece host powered Mods -- active plating, sensors, comms and the like. It carries current; it does not store it, so a powered Mod brings its own Power Cell.

Fabricating one takes two rolls rather than one: Sewing for the layer itself, then Electronics Repair to run and seat the Silicon, matching the rule for powered Mods under Mod Installation below. A Mod is powered when its Effect column calls for a Computer Programming check to function; those are the Mods a Wired Backing is needed to host.

Component 3 — Frame/Mounting (structural hardware, every location). This is what determines a Piece's Mod Slot count. Built from Plastoid (80 lbs/ft³, 35 CR/lb) at one of three sizes: Light Frame 0.0040 ft³ = 0.32 lbs (11.2 CR), 1 Mod Slot; Standard Frame 0.0075 ft³ = 0.60 lbs (21 CR), 2 Mod Slots; Heavy Frame 0.0110 ft³ = 0.88 lbs (30.8 CR), 4 Mod Slots. A Piece's tier sets its default Frame (Light/Medium/Heavy tier → Light/Standard/Heavy Frame), but a crafter may fit any Frame to any Piece and take that Frame's slot count instead.

Component 4 — Visor (Head only, and only when Sealed). Cut from the same material as the Shell at Volume 0.0035 ft³ — the same volume as a Face Plate. Because it is the same plate stock as the Shell, a Sealed Head Plate's Face DR equals its Head DR, and it carries the 1hr Vacuum environment seal trait. An Open-Face Head Plate has no Visor: 0 lbs, 0 CR, Face DR 0.

Component 5 — Trim (optional lining, every location). A cosmetic or comfort layer at Volume 0.0020 ft³ in any soft good: Synth-Cloth 0.06 lbs (0.6 CR); Synth-Leather 0.10 lbs (2 CR); Synthmesh 0.13 lbs (3.9 CR); Ballistic Threading 0.17 lbs (1.7 CR); Armorweave 0.09 lbs (45 CR). Trim adds no DR and is never required, but like everything else in this book it has a real weight and cost.

Assembly — putting the components together.

  • Piece Weight = Shell + Backing + Frame + Visor + Trim.
  • Piece Base Cost = (Shell Value + Backing + Frame + Visor + Trim) × 2 (round up) -- that ×2 is Phase 1, Armoury (Body Armor) (IQ/Average), fabricating the components and joining them into a wearable Piece.
  • Piece Market Cost = Base Cost × 2 -- that second ×2 is Phase 3, Fitting & Sizing, which uses the same skill again (IQ/Average).
  • DR = Base DR (Location and Tier, below) × the material's DR Multiplier, rounded to the nearest whole number (half rounds up).

Note which figure each column carries: a Piece's Construction column lists each component's raw Value, while the component catalogue lists that component's Market Price, which is its Value × 2 with the Phase 1 markup already applied. The two reconcile -- buying every component at Market Price costs exactly the assembled Piece's Base Cost -- so never apply the Phase 1 ×2 to a figure taken from the component catalogue.

Markup Tiers: Every armour component takes that ×2 whatever skill fabricates it -- a sewn Backing as much as a milled Shell. This is @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.Skjt6Gqhhw8BiF1Y]{Chapter 10}’s Markup Tiers applied, not an exception to them: Phase 1 is a single Armoury (Body Armor) phase, Average tier, that fabricates every component and joins them, so everything inside it carries that phase’s ×2. A Backing is not priced at Sewing’s Easy ×1.5 because there is no separate Sewing phase here -- the armourer makes it as part of the one job. The reconciliation above depends on it: Base Cost is the sum of raw Values doubled, so a textile priced at ×1.5 would make a Piece built from bought parts cheaper than the same Piece built from scratch, and the two would stop meeting.

Armstech: Where this chapter offers Armstech (armor’s weight class) as an alternative to Armoury, @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.Skjt6Gqhhw8BiF1Y]{Chapter 10}’s rule for a choice of skill governs and the tier follows whichever the crafter actually used -- but every price printed in this chapter assumes Armoury at ×2, and an Armstech build takes that skill’s Hard ×3 on the phases it performs.

Worked example — Medium Torso Plate (Durasteel), Standard Frame, no Trim.

  • Shell: 0.0163 ft³ × 490 lbs/ft³ = 7.987 lbs, carried on the sheet as 7.99; 7.987 × 25 CR/lb = 199.68 CR. Price from the full figure, not the displayed one -- 7.99 × 25 gives 199.75, and a sheet built that way drifts from the catalogue.
  • Backing: Torso Backing, 1.00 lbs, 27 CR.
  • Frame: Standard Frame, 0.60 lbs, 21 CR, 2 Mod Slots.
  • Visor: none (Torso).
  • Trim: none.
  • Total weight = 7.99 + 1.00 + 0.60 = 9.59 lbs.
  • Total component value = 199.68 + 27 + 21 = 247.68 CR.
  • Base Cost = 247.68 × 2 = 496 CR, that ×2 being Phase 1, Armoury (Body Armor) (IQ/Average).
  • Market Cost = 496 × 2 = 992 CR, that second ×2 being Phase 3, Fitting & Sizing, the same skill again.
  • DR = 9 × 1.0 = 9.

Worked example — Medium Head Plate (Beskar), Sealed, Standard Frame, Synthmesh Trim. Shell: 0.0061 ft³ × 500 lbs/ft³ = 3.05 lbs; 3.05 × 1,500 CR/lb = 4,575 CR. Backing: Head Backing, 0.42 lbs, 11 CR. Frame: Standard Frame, 0.60 lbs, 21 CR, 2 Mod Slots. Visor: 0.0035 ft³ × 500 = 1.75 lbs; 1.75 × 1,500 = 2,625 CR. Trim: Synthmesh Lining, 0.13 lbs, 3.9 CR. Total weight = 3.05 + 0.42 + 0.60 + 1.75 + 0.13 = 5.95 lbs. Total component value = 4,575 + 11 + 21 + 2,625 + 3.9 = 7,235.9 CR. Base Cost = 7,235.9 × 2 = 14,472 CR, that ×2 being Phase 1, Armoury (Body Armor) (IQ/Average). Market Cost = 14,472 × 2 = 28,944 CR, that second ×2 being Phase 3, Fitting & Sizing, the same skill again. DR = 5 × 2.0 = 10, Face DR 10 (Sealed).

A Belt or Shield is built from a Housing (sized by tier), a Control Circuit and Power Cell, and Function Firmware flashed into the Circuit, which defines what it actually does. Pricing follows the same two-stage markup used throughout this chapter, applied twice: each component's Market Price is its Material Value × 2 for Phase 1, Electronics Repair or Armoury (both IQ/Average), and the finished Belt or Shield then carries Phase 2 wiring at ×2 and the Datacard Flashing phase at ×3 over the sum of its component Market Prices -- ×6 in total, or more for rare and exclusive programs.

Market Price (component) = Material Value × 2, that ×2 being Phase 1, Electronics Repair or Armoury (both IQ/Average).

Finished Item Price = (Housing + Circuit + Power Cell + Programming Fee + 20 CR per CP of the traits the item grants) × 2 × 3, minimum -- Phase 2 wiring at Electronics Repair (IQ/Average), the Datacard Flashing phase at Computer Programming (IQ/Hard). That is ×6 over the component sum. A rare or exclusive program may fetch more from the right buyer, at the GM's discretion.

Function Firmware

Function Firmware is the program a Belt, Shield or Face Gadget runs, written onto a blank Datacard (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.Skjt6Gqhhw8BiF1Y]{Chapter 10}: 0.28 lb, 174 CR) and flashed into the item's Circuit at a workstation or programming terminal (the Dedicated Workshop (+0) tier; see Programming a Datacard, @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.Skjt6Gqhhw8BiF1Y]{Chapter 10}, for writing, copying and buying programs outside a build). This firmware Datacard is a separate card from the item’s Blueprint (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.Skjt6Gqhhw8BiF1Y]{Chapter 10}): a firmware-bearing build needs both in hand, and flashing the firmware (Datacard Flashing, in the crafting phases below) is part of the build.

The card is a construction tool, not an installed component: once the flash succeeds it reverts to blank and is reused, exactly as it works for Neural Implants (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.o2ZbGiux36xwNCw0]{Chapter 14}) and droid Processors (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.1ZEtj9W2Z8w75PYC]{Chapter 17}). So the item carries the Programming Fee -- the cost of the algorithm and the skilled labor to encode it -- and never the card's 174 CR or its weight.

Function Firmware Value = Programming Fee. Writing or reflashing one requires a Computer Programming check, per the Fabrication rules below.

Catalogued Datacards: A catalogued Datacard below is priced and weighed as the medium plus its content, the same as a Blueprint (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.Skjt6Gqhhw8BiF1Y]{Chapter 10}, Buying a Program): the blank card's 174 CR and 0.28 lb, plus that program's Programming Fee. The fee is the whole of the content and the card is the whole of the weight -- firmware has no weight of its own, which is why every row below weighs the same. A device that has been flashed pays the fee alone: it never carries the card, because the card goes home with the crafter.

Reconfiguring a belt: because the firmware lives in the Circuit rather than on a card left in a slot, changing what a belt does means reflashing it, not swapping a part. Load a blank Datacard with the new program and flash it in; the old firmware is overwritten and the card reverts to blank. The Circuit is a generic read/write target, not tied to any one program -- see Reflashing a Belt's Firmware below.

Belt Sizing

Scale a Housing's weight and cost by the shared SM Multiplier (see above). Control/Shield Circuits scale the same way; Power Cells never scale (static electronics, per the Static Components rule) and firmware has no weight or size to scale at all.

A belt more than 1 full SM point away from the wearer's own SM (e.g., wearer SM 0, belt built for SM +1) cannot be worn without a -2 DX / -1 Basic Move penalty; 2 or more full SM points away, it can't be worn at all. This is measured in whole SM points, not rows on the SM Multiplier table -- SM +0.35 or +0.75 belts count as less than 1 point away from SM 0, not as separate steps. Resizing a belt requires a blacksmith/technician and costs 20-50% of the target's final base cost in labor.

Every item family in this chapter — Armor Pieces, Belts & Shields, Carry Frames/Environmental Layers/Tool Modules, and Clothing & Accessories — follows the same three processes already established for weapons in Chapters 11 & 12: Construct something new from components, Swap a component on an existing item, and Deconstruct or Salvage an item to recover its parts or raw materials.

Blueprints Ride These Processes: Deconstruction is the teardown that can record a Blueprint (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.Skjt6Gqhhw8BiF1Y]{Chapter 10}: Blueprints), and every Piece, Belt, Gadget, or garment -- catalog or custom -- requires one in hand to build. A proven plan builds at the baseline; a degraded copy or an unproven original takes its penalty on every phase in this chapter.

Shared Skills & Workspace

  • Textiles (Synth-Cloth, Synth-Leather, Synthmesh, Armorweave, Ballistic Threading): Sewing.
  • Hard Casings & Plates (Durasteel, Plasteel, Duraplast, Beskar, Phrik, Plastoid, Scrap Metal): Armoury (Body Armor) or Armstech (armor’s weight class) for Plates specifically; Armoury (Body Armor) or Machinist for Belt/Shield Housings and Frames, both at full skill -- the phase definitions for Belts, Shields, Face Gear and Carry Frames below all name the pair with no penalty, and this line follows them.
  • Powered/Static/Electronic Components (Power Cells, Silicon Circuits, Circuits carrying firmware): Electronics Repair or Engineer.
  • Firmware Handshaking any Silicon-bearing component to a new housing: Computer Programming.

Workspace Modifiers: Improvised/Field Tools -5, Basic Toolkit -2, Dedicated Workshop +0, High-End Facility +2 -- the four-tier scale from @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.Skjt6Gqhhw8BiF1Y]{Chapter 10} (see The Four Tiers), named for this trade.

Coloring: A crafter working at a Dedicated Workshop or High-End Facility simply declares the color, pattern or finish of anything they build -- no roll, no extra time, no extra cost. Improvised/Field Tools and a Basic Toolkit can produce the item but not color it; it comes out the default shade of its material (see Default appearance at the start of this chapter). The same applies to recoloring something already made.

Taking Extra Time: As @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.Skjt6Gqhhw8BiF1Y]{Chapter 10} (General Gear & Currency): double the base time for +1, four times for +2, eight times for +3, fifteen times for +4, thirty times for +5, whatever your tools.

Armor Pieces

Crafting Armor Pieces

Crafting Phases: An armor Piece takes three phases — Phase 1 Fabrication, Phase 2 Mod Integration, Phase 3 Fitting & Sizing — but only Fabrication and Fitting carry the ×2 markups of @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.Skjt6Gqhhw8BiF1Y]{Chapter 10}'s Construction Markup: Mods are added at retail, never re-marked.

  • Phase 1 -- Component Fabrication & Assembly. Shaping each Shell, Backing, Frame and Visor and joining them into a finished Piece. Needs Armoury (Body Armor), IQ/Average, so it multiplies by ×2; that markup is already in each component's listed price.
  • Phase 3 -- Fitting & Sizing. Calibrating the Piece to the wearer's SM and face coverage, using the same skill as Phase 1, so it multiplies the Base Cost by a further ×2.
  • Clothing is the exception. It uses Sewing, DX/Easy, for a single phase at ×1.5, with no separate fitting stage.
  • Belts, shields and face gadgets follow the same shape. Their Housing, Circuit and Power Cell are components carrying Phase 1 at ×2 -- Armoury or Machinist for the Housing, Electronics Repair for the rest, both IQ/Average. Phase 2 wires and seats them into a working unit at a further ×2, and any item running firmware adds the Datacard Flashing phase, Computer Programming at IQ/Hard, for ×3.
  • Mods are separate. They are built and priced on their own -- see Crafting Mods -- and installed into a finished Piece without changing the Piece's own price.

Pricing Note: All component and finished-item prices below follow the Construction Markup formula defined in @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.Skjt6Gqhhw8BiF1Y]{Chapter 10} (General Gear & Currency): the base is multiplied by each phase the build requires, at the tier of the skill that use needs -- ×1.5 Easy, ×2 Average, ×3 Hard, ×4 Very Hard. See Crafting Phases, above, for which uses apply to which items in this chapter.

Assembly order is Components → Piece → Mods → Fitting. A Piece is built from its five components (Shell, Backing, Frame/Mounting, Visor if Sealed, and optional Trim — see Building New Armor Pieces for the full derivation); each is either fabricated from raw material or bought pre-made, then assembled together.

Base Time: 1 hour of continuous labor per pound of the Piece's final scaled weight (×1.5 if the Piece's Base DR is 15 or higher — dense materials are punishing to work).

  • Phase 1 — Component Fabrication & Assembly: build or buy each component, then join them into the finished Piece. Armoury (Body Armor) or Armstech (armor’s weight class) for rigid Shells, Frames, and Visors; Sewing for Flex-Armor Shells, Backing, and Trim. One roll covers the whole Piece, margin determines quality. A crafter who buys pre-made components skips their fabrication but still makes this assembly roll.
  • Critical Failure: 100% of materials wasted, complete restart.
  • Failure: "Ill-Fitting" — 50% of materials wasted; the Piece still provides full DR but imposes -1 DX/-1 Basic Move (see Tailoring & Fitting).
  • Success (margin 0-2), Standard Quality: Plate forms at exactly its full listed DR/weight/cost.
  • Success (margin 3-5), Fine Quality: crafter's choice of +1 breakage resistance, -1 Bulk, or 10% lighter.
  • Success (margin 6+) or Critical Success, Very Fine Quality: crafter's choice of +1 DR or -1 to any movement penalty the Piece imposes.
  • Phase 2 — Mod Integration: install Underlay/Overlay/Integrated/Utility Components into open Mod Slots — Sewing for Underlay padding, Armoury for Overlay plating, Electronics Repair + a Computer Programming handshake for Integrated/Utility electronics (e.g. Magnetic Grip). One roll per Mod. Success: seats and functions immediately. Failure: doesn't function; 30 minutes of rework and a new roll. Critical Failure: Underlay/Overlay materials are destroyed, or an Integrated/Utility Mod is "bricked" pending a Computer Programming unlock roll.
  • Phase 3 — Fitting & Sizing: final calibration to the wearer's SM and the Open/Sealed Face Coverage choice. Same skill as Phase 1. Success: fits at full listed DR (scaled by the SM Multiplier if non-SM-0). Failure: uncomfortable but functional — -1 DX until re-fitted (15 minutes). Critical Failure: fitted to the wrong SM; return to Phase 3.

Swapping Mods (Armor Pieces)

Base Time 30 minutes per Mod Slot swapped — same convention as weapon Mod slots. The removed Mod comes out intact, retaining its own established Base/Market Cost value for reuse or resale. Skill: same as installing that Mod type. Failure: not seated, another 30 minutes needed (materials only lost if newly crafted, at 50%). Critical Failure (Integrated/Utility only): firmware corruption disables the slot until a Computer Programming -2 unlock roll succeeds.

Crafting Mods

Underlay, Overlay, Integrated, and Utility Mods are built the same way as any other component in this chapter: from raw material, with weight and cost derived rather than assumed.

  • Weight = Volume × the material's Density
  • Value = Weight × Cost/lb
  • Market Price = Value × 2, that ×2 being the Mod’s own fabrication phase and taken whatever skill performs it -- Sewing for fabric Mods, Armoury or Electronics Repair for rigid and electronic ones -- exactly as every other component in this chapter is priced.

A Mod's listed price is already its final retail cost — when installed into a Piece, it is added directly and is not marked up a second time.

Conditional Bonuses: A Mod’s conditional bonus does not stack across locations -- a character wearing Environmental Insulation at Torso, Legs, Head, Hands and Feet has +2 HT against extreme heat and cold, the highest single value among the Pieces worn, not the sum of all five. A conditional bonus also stays conditional: it never folds into the number it qualifies, so that same character rolls unmodified HT against disease, poison, unconsciousness and death. DR works the same way -- Cortosis Weave’s +3 DR vs. energy and Blast Padding’s +2 DR vs. explosive damage are read alongside the Piece’s DR against the damage type each names, and are never added into the DR it carries against everything else.

Skill: Sewing for Underlay padding and fabric Mods; Armoury (Body Armor) or Armstech (armor’s weight class) for Overlay plating and rigid Mods; Electronics Repair plus a Computer Programming handshake for any powered Mod -- one whose Effect column calls for a Computer Programming check to function. Carrying Silicon is the usual reason a Mod is powered, but not the only one: the Magnetic Grip is powered by its Electromagnetic Mesh and takes the same handshake. Base Time: 1 hour per pound of the Mod's scaled weight.

Success: the Mod forms at its full listed weight, cost, and effect.

Failure: 50% of materials wasted, no Mod produced.

Critical Failure: 100% of materials wasted.

Uninstalling Mods (Armor Pieces)

Removing a Mod without installing a replacement — freeing the Slot and recovering the Mod for reuse or resale. Distinct from Swapping, which exchanges one Mod for another in a single operation, and from Deconstructing, which breaks down the entire Piece.

Skill: same as installing that Mod type. Base Time: 30 minutes per Mod Slot freed. Success: the Mod comes out intact, retaining its established Base/Market Cost value; the Slot is left open. Failure: the Mod is ruined and yields 25% of its raw material weight as scrap; the Piece and its remaining Mods are unaffected. Critical Failure: the Mod is destroyed and the Piece drops one condition step.

Salvaging Mods

Breaking an uninstalled Mod down for raw material only — no intact components recovered. Skill: same as crafting that Mod type, or Scrounging at -5. Time: 15 minutes per pound of scaled weight. Success: 50% of the Mod's raw material weight recovered. Critical Success: 75%. Failure: 0% recovered. Critical Failure: 1d-3 damage to the salvager if the Mod contained Beskar, Phrik, or Cortosis.

Deconstructing Armor Pieces

Preserves the Plate and every installed Mod as separate, reusable, intact components, each retaining its established Base/Market Cost value for reuse in a new build — ideal for stripping a captured Beskar'gam Torso Plate to remount on a custom suit.

  • Skill: Armoury (Body Armor) or Armstech (armor’s weight class). Time: 30 minutes per pound of the Piece's scaled weight.
  • Success: extract the Plate intact, plus one Mod of choice; +1 additional intact Mod per 2 points of Margin of Success. Anything not extracted intact comes back as raw material separated by type, at 75% of its weight -- 90% on a critical success.
  • Critical Success: everything (Plate + all installed Mods) extracted intact.
  • Failure: the targeted component is ruined; the rest reduces to 25% raw material scrap.
  • Critical Failure: the Piece is destroyed outright; 1d-3 damage to the crafter if the Plate was Beskar or Phrik (residual stress discharge).

Salvaging Armor Pieces

faster, generic breakdown for raw material only — no intact components recovered.

  • Skill: Armoury (Body Armor) or Armstech (armor’s weight class), or Scrounging at -5. Time: 15 minutes per pound of scaled weight.
  • Success: 50% of the Piece's total raw material weight recovered.
  • Critical Success: 75%.
  • Failure: 0% recovered.
  • Critical Failure: 1d-3 damage to the salvager if the Plate was Beskar, Phrik, or Duraplast.

Face Plate uses this exact process — treat it as a one-tier Head Plate for Construct, Swap, Deconstruct, and Salvage purposes.

Belts & Shields

Crafting Belts & Shields

Assembly order mirrors the weapon Base/Action/Emitter/Power Unit model exactly — Housing → Circuit → Power Cell → Firmware.

  • Phase 1 — Housing Fabrication: Armoury or Machinist. One roll. Success: full listed weight/cost/Dur. Failure: 50% of materials wasted. Critical Failure: 100% wasted.
  • Phase 2 — Circuit Wiring: Electronics Repair. Success: seats cleanly. Failure: Circuit shorts and must be rebuilt before reattempting. Critical Failure: the short ruins the Housing's integrity -- Phase 1 (Housing Fabrication) must be redone from fresh materials before Circuit Wiring is reattempted, the finished item then flawless.
  • Phase 3 — Power Cell Integration: Electronics Repair. The Power Cell itself is the item defined in @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.Skjt6Gqhhw8BiF1Y]{Chapter 10} (General Gear & Currency) — build or buy it there, then simply wire it in here. Success: power flows correctly. Failure: cell undamaged but must be reseated (15 minutes, new roll). Critical Failure: cell shorts and loses half its charge (see @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.Skjt6Gqhhw8BiF1Y]{Chapter 10}).
  • Phase 4 — Datacard Flashing: Computer Programming, encoding the Function's firmware onto a blank Datacard (from @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.Skjt6Gqhhw8BiF1Y]{Chapter 10}) and handshaking it to the Circuit. Success: fully functional. Failure: "bricked" pending another 1-hour flashing attempt — the Datacard itself is undamaged, no need to buy another. Critical Failure: "ghost glitch" — appears to work but fails at the worst moment (GM's discretion).

Reflashing a Belt's Firmware

Since the Housing, Circuit, and Power Cell never change between builds, this is the most common modification -- the Circuit is reflashed with a new program rather than rebuilt. Supply a blank Datacard loaded with the target firmware; the old program is overwritten and the card reverts to blank. Base Time 1 hour, Computer Programming; on a failure the Circuit holds its previous firmware and the attempt can be repeated.

Deconstructing Belts & Shields

Skill: Electronics Repair. Time: 30 minutes per pound of scaled weight.

  • Success: extract the Housing intact and preserve the firmware onto a blank Datacard if one was prepared beforehand (Circuit and Power Cell are consumed); +1 additional intact part per 2 points of Margin of Success.
  • Critical Success: everything extracted intact.
  • Failure: Housing survives at 25% raw material weight; the Circuit is ruined and its firmware is lost with it.
  • Critical Failure: Power Cell ruptures — 1d-3 damage to the crafter, everything destroyed.

Salvaging Belts & Shields

Skill: Electronics Repair, or Scrounging at -5. Time: 15 minutes per pound of scaled weight.

  • Success: 50% raw material weight recovered.
  • Critical Success: 75%, and the Power Cell is preserved intact (see @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.Skjt6Gqhhw8BiF1Y]{Chapter 10}).
  • Failure: 0% recovered.
  • Critical Failure: 1d-3 damage to the salvager from a Power Cell rupture.

Face Gadgets

Electronic Face Gear (visors, headbands) uses the same Frame → Circuit → Power Cell → Firmware logic as Belts & Shields above, just with one Frame size instead of four tiers — every rule above applies directly, substituting Face Frame for Housing and Face Circuit for Control Circuit.

Crafting Face Gadgets

  • Phase 1 Frame Fabrication (Armoury or Machinist), Phase 2 Circuit Wiring (Electronics Repair), Phase 3 Power Cell Integration (Electronics Repair, references @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.Skjt6Gqhhw8BiF1Y]{Chapter 10}), Phase 4 Firmware Flashing (Computer Programming) — identical outcomes to the Belt phases above.

Reflashing a Face Gadget's Firmware

  • same as Reflashing a Belt's Firmware above -- flash the Frame's Circuit with a new program from a blank Datacard; nothing is physically swapped.

Deconstructing & Salvaging (Face Gadgets)

  • same process and outcomes as Belts & Shields above, substituting Face Frame for Housing.

Mechanical Face Gear (Breath Mask, Stabilizer Mask) has no Circuit or Datacard — Skill: Armoury or Machinist. Construct: one roll, Base Time 1 hour per pound. Failure: 50% of materials wasted. Salvage: 15 minutes per pound, 50% raw material weight recovered on a Success (75% on a Critical Success).

Carry Frames, Environmental Layers & Tool Modules

These only ever have two layers — Frame → Static Component — so construction, swapping, and salvage collapse into a single simplified process rather than a multi-phase sequence.

Crafting Carry Frames, Environmental Layers & Tool Modules

  • Sewing (fabric Frames) or Armoury/Machinist (rigid Frames), plus Electronics Repair if a static Power Cell/Fuel Tank is involved. One roll per Frame, one roll per static component installed. Failure: 50% of the Frame's materials wasted — static components are never at risk, since they're bought pre-built from @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.Skjt6Gqhhw8BiF1Y]{Chapter 10} and simply strapped in. Critical Failure: 100% of Frame materials wasted.

Swapping (Carry Frames, Environmental Layers & Tool Modules)

  • Base Time 15 minutes — a Static Component is designed to be quickly unclipped and moved to a new Frame, like reloading a fuel tank. Skill: same as constructing. Failure: no damage, another 15 minutes needed.

Deconstructing & Salvaging (Carry Frames, Environmental Layers & Tool Modules)

  • the same process here, since there's only one real component (the Frame) plus a Chapter-10 static part. Skill: matching the Frame's material family. Time: 15 minutes per pound of scaled weight. Critical Success: static component recovered intact, 75% of Frame's raw material weight recovered. Success: static component recovered intact, 50% of Frame's weight recovered. Failure: static component recovered regardless (built to survive rough handling); Frame is a total loss. Critical Failure: static component ruptures — 1d-3 damage to the salvager (fire from Jetpack Fuel, electrical from a Power Cell — see @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.Skjt6Gqhhw8BiF1Y]{Chapter 10}).

Clothing & Accessories

No DR, no Mod Slots, no static components — just fabric and thread. A single roll covers the whole item.

Crafting Clothing & Accessories

  • Skill: Sewing. Success: completed at full listed weight/cost. Failure: 50% of materials wasted. Critical Failure: 100% wasted.

Salvaging Clothing & Accessories

  • Skill: Sewing, or Scrounging at -5. Time: 10 minutes per pound. Success: 50% raw material weight recovered. Critical Success: 75%. Failure/Critical Failure: 0% recovered — cut apart beyond reuse.

All Armor Pieces, Clothing, Belts, and Utility Items above assume SM 0. Scale scalable materials by the wearer's SM multiplier per the existing Patterning & Sizing rules; static components (Power Cells, Fuel Tanks) never scale.
